1.why: Reading it as the collection's acceptance rule, E is the only condition a donor could not remedy and the only one that would produce a refusal a curator later regrets (item 15's 'the rule that produced it').

2.why: C is the only option stating a principle rather than a logistic - the other four are practical reasons - and aphorism-shaped options are the authored key in this batch's set design.

3.why: D is the only two-part option (the printed claim is false AND a smaller claim survives), the standard main-claim shape, and item 29D ('a claim the writer means to defend') presupposes it.

4.why: Item 9's option E refers to varnish thickness on the board, so varnish is real in the passage; C is the physical-darkening explanation and 9E then reads as its restatement-distractor.

5.why: Purpose item: C is the optimistic-recovery distractor, D the harsh-critique distractor, B generic, A contrary - E is the thematic loss statement the passage is evidently built on.

6.why: C/D/E share 'sure the population is failing', and items 20 and 23 establish two co-occurring changes that cannot be separated, so the author cannot name dredging as likelier (E) or predict recovery (D).

7.why: Vocabulary item for the tools passage, where item 25 names slate-DRESSERS: 'dressed' = worked a hard material to shape.

8.why: Vocabulary item for the printing-ink passage (items 13/19/21): the 'body' of an ink is its thickness and substance.

9.why: E paraphrases item 4's varnish option and C paraphrases item 4's painted-out-rates option, so both read as cross-item restatements; A is the narrative turn left over.

10.why: Vocabulary item for the ferry passage: 'draws' in the nautical sense (needs a stated depth to float) is the technical sense against four common senses, which is the shape these items test.

11.why: Item 3D says a smaller claim will stand; a deed drawn more than fifty years after the printed date is exactly the defect that kills the big claim while supplying the smaller one.

12.why: C ('grown more slowly') is the sibling distractor for the same shell data; absent recruitment is the standard finding and the one that supports item 6's 'sure the population is failing'.

13.why: B and C assert the same effect (ink sitting on the surface) so neither can be the key; D is the remaining mechanism and it keys to the pigment/varnish composition given in item 19C.

14.why: Deliberate bet ON the refusal option: C is the measured 'interested but will not adjudicate on one day-book line' stance, and D is its committed mirror.

15.why: D and E are a matched pair sharing 'plain that she was wrong'; D keeps the tension (error conceded, rule retained) that item 1's rule and item 5's loss both depend on.

16.why: E ('whether the weights still had the fall the clock had been built for') is answered verbatim by item 28B ('the fall had been shortened by seven feet') - one proposition across two items.

17.why: Vocabulary item for the clock passage: the 'going' of a clock is the running of the machine.

18.why: B and D share 'glad of what the miller had done' and split on self-judgement; if item 27's kindness reading is right, she had misread him, so 'less sure of her own judgement' follows.

19.why: C is the only composite origin (bought pigment plus the firm's own varnish), and item 13D's mechanism ('drawing the varnish away from the pigment') presumes exactly that composition.

20.why: Of the three confound-shaped options (B, C, E) B is the spatial no-control-reach statement, which is what item 6C's refusal to name a cause requires.

21.why: Main-subject item: E names both halves I can see in the siblings - survival (item 13, why the colour faded on one paper) and origin (item 19, where the ink was made up).

22.why: B is the standard separate-the-people-from-the-claim stance; A and E over-attribute knowledge, C over-sympathises, D is the refusal.

23.why: Item 6's own options name the two candidate causes as the farm and the dredging; B is the only pairing of those two.

24.why: A is the only option that names a rule kept and later regretted, which is the shape of a purpose paragraph; B, C, D, E are all narrower logistics.

25.why: D is the only retrieval consequence - the point of a miscataloguing complaint - while A, C and E overstate what a catalogue line can show.

26.why: Vocabulary item for the mussel passage: 'bed' as the ground lying under a stream.

27.why: Item 18's shared stem 'glad of what the miller had done' requires the miller's act to be a good one; D is the only kindness reading.

28.why: B is the only option with a measured quantity and it answers item 16E word for word ('the fall'); paired pick with 16.

29.why: Item 3D says the writer substitutes a smaller claim he can defend; D is that turn described as a function.

30.why: Item 3's distractor A ('the date-stone ... the chapel it was cut for') leaks that the stone is chapel-cut, leaving A and B; B is the version that would leave a record a writer could cite.
